papers.title: Single Molecule Diffusion Studies Reveal Rapid Translations Across Target Membrane Surfaces for both p40Phox PX domain and Class III PI3K VPS34 Complex 1, the Autophagy Lipid Kinase
papers.summary: This study uses single-molecule imaging to watch how two proteins involved in autophagy—the p40Phox PX domain and the VPS34 Complex 1 lipid kinase—move across membrane surfaces. The researchers found that both proteins diffuse and translate rapidly across their target membranes rather than staying fixed in place. This fast movement likely helps these proteins efficiently find and act on specific lipid targets needed to kick off autophagy processes.
papers.why: Since VPS34 and its lipid signaling are core machinery for initiating autophagy, understanding its membrane dynamics during autophagy initiation could inform how mitophagy is regulated in neurons, a central theme of this PhD project.
papers.figure: The figure showing single-molecule tracking trajectories and diffusion coefficients of p40Phox PX domain and VPS34 Complex 1 on membrane surfaces.

papers.title: Lutein inhibits ATF3-mediated PINK1/Parkin signaling to modulate neuronal mitophagy and alleviate Parkinson's disease progression.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how lutein, a natural compound, affects neuronal mitophagy in Parkinson's disease by blocking a signaling pathway involving the proteins ATF3, PINK1, and Parkin. These proteins normally help cells identify and remove damaged mitochondria, a process known as mitophagy that is often disrupted in Parkinson's disease. The study shows that lutein can modulate this pathway to reduce disease progression, likely by restoring more balanced mitophagy levels in neurons.
papers.why: This paper's focus on PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy in neurons is directly relevant to the PhD project's core theme of mitophagy and autophagy regulation in brain neurons.

papers.title: Nanomaterial modulation of lysosomal homeostasis in neurodegenerative proteinopathies: from pathological-protein degradation to re-release and seeding.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how engineered nanomaterials interact with lysosomes in cells affected by neurodegenerative diseases, where misfolded proteins like tau, alpha-synuclein, or amyloid-beta accumulate. It discusses how nanomaterials can either help degrade these pathological proteins or, problematically, disrupt lysosomal function and cause the proteins to be re-released from cells, potentially spreading disease. The review likely covers both therapeutic potential and risks of nanomaterial-based interventions targeting the lysosomal degradation pathway.
papers.why: Since lysosomal function is the terminal step of autophagy and mitophagy, understanding how nanomaterials disrupt or enhance this pathway is directly relevant to studying neuronal proteostasis and could inform therapeutic strategies tested in your interneuron and perineuronal net models.

papers.title: Bisphenol S facilitates breast cancer progression through DRP1-mediated mitophagy.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how bisphenol S, a common plastic additive, promotes breast cancer growth by altering mitochondrial dynamics. It focuses on DRP1, a protein that controls mitochondrial fission, and shows it drives mitophagy (selective degradation of mitochondria) in cancer cells. The study links environmental chemical exposure to cancer progression via this mitochondrial quality control pathway.
papers.why: While focused on breast cancer rather than neurons, this paper's mechanistic insights into DRP1-mediated mitophagy could inform understanding of mitochondrial quality control pathways relevant to neuronal mitophagy research.

papers.title: Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteomics Reveals Extensive Remodeling Following Autophagy-Lysosomal Flux Inhibition in Preimplantation Mouse Embryos.
papers.summary: This study uses mass spectrometry-based proteomics to examine how blocking autophagy-lysosomal flux affects protein composition in early mouse embryos before implantation. The researchers found extensive remodeling of the proteome when this degradation pathway is inhibited, suggesting autophagy plays a major role in shaping protein content during this developmental stage. This provides a comprehensive, unbiased dataset of proteins affected by autophagy disruption in embryos.
papers.why: While focused on embryos rather than neurons, this paper offers methodological insights into using proteomics to study autophagy-lysosomal flux inhibition, which could inform approaches for studying mitophagy/autophagy pathways in neuronal contexts.

papers.title: Research progress of mitophagy and its targeted therapeutic strategies in rheumatoid arthritis.
papers.summary: This paper reviews current knowledge on mitophagy, the process by which cells selectively degrade damaged mitochondria, in the context of rheumatoid arthritis. It discusses how dysregulated mitophagy contributes to disease progression in joint tissues and immune cells. The review also covers emerging therapeutic strategies that aim to target mitophagy pathways for treating rheumatoid arthritis.
papers.why: While focused on a peripheral autoimmune disease rather than neurons, this review could offer mechanistic insights into mitophagy pathway regulation and targeted therapeutic strategies potentially transferable to neuronal mitophagy research.

papers.title: Pharmacological activation of mitophagy prevents calcific aortic valve disease by targeting dysregulated mitochondrial-to-nuclear communication
papers.summary: This study investigates how impaired mitophagy, the process of clearing damaged mitochondria, contributes to calcific aortic valve disease. The researchers found that mitochondrial dysfunction disrupts communication with the nucleus, triggering harmful gene expression changes in valve cells. Using a drug that pharmacologically boosts mitophagy, they were able to restore healthy mitochondrial-nuclear signaling and prevent calcification in the valve tissue.
papers.why: While focused on cardiovascular tissue rather than neurons, this paper offers mechanistic insight into pharmacological activation of mitophagy and its downstream effects on mitochondrial-to-nuclear communication, which could inform therapeutic strategies relevant to mitophagy dysfunction in neuronal and interneuron biology.
